evidence: Cic. Att. 15.16a.1: itaque mē referunt pedēs in Tusculānum
Sen. Ep. 55.11: itaque mēcum studē, mēcum cēnā, mēcum ambulā
terms.comment: “And so”: what follows from the facts just told. It stands first in its clause; later in the sentence only from Livy on (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: adverb, usually second in its clause
evidence: Cic. Att. 13.42.3: diem meum scīs esse III Nōnās Jānuāriās; aderis igitur
terms.comment: “So, then”: a conclusion drawn, or a return to the point (sīc igitur vīvitur, so this is how we live: Cic. Fam. 9.26.3). In classical prose it usually follows the first word (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: then, so (above all in questions and requests)
evidence: Plaut. Rud. 184b: Sequere mē hāc ergō.
Cic. Att. 12.1.2: quid ergō opus erat epistulā?
terms.comment: The “then” of talk: quid ergō?, what then?; venī ergō mēcum, come with me, then (Phaedr. 3.7.15).

terms.gloss: and so, for this reason (leading to a request or advice)
evidence: Cic. Fam. 1.10.1: quā rē fac ut quam prīmum veniās
Quint. 1.4.12: quārē discat puer, quid in litterīs proprium, quid commūne
terms.comment: “For which reason”: in Cicero’s letters it leads into the request, quā rē velim …; the Perseus text of the letters prints it as two words.

phrases.latin: hoc igitur habēbis, novī nihil. quid ergō opus erat epistulā?
phrases.english: so there you have it: no news. Then why write at all?

phrases.latin: itaque mē referunt pedēs in Tusculānum
phrases.english: and so my feet are carrying me back to Tusculum
Follow me this way, then. — I’m coming.

sources: Lewis & Short: itaque · Lewis & Short: igitur · Lewis & Short: ergo · Lewis & Short: quare
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 393.
